---
title: "Covariates and the time grid"
---

The emulator takes twelve numbers. They describe the setting as it stands and the campaign
being evaluated, and together they are everything the model is told about a district.

## The twelve covariates

The names and their canonical order are carried in the checkpoint itself.

```{python}
from stateMINT.model import Mamba2Regressor

artifact = Mamba2Regressor.from_pretrained(
    "dide-ic/stateMINT", predictor="prevalence", revision="v1.2.2",
)

for i, name in enumerate(artifact.preprocessing_config["static_covars"], start=1):
    print(f"{i:2d}. {name}")
```

Pass them as a dictionary, one per scenario, and the order above takes care of itself. Note
that all twelve keys must be present.

| Covariate | Meaning | Range | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|---|
| `eir` | Infectious bites per person per year | > 0, roughly 0.1–200 | [estiMINT](../04-estimint/estimating-eir.qmd), from a measured prevalence |
| `dn0_use` | Probability a mosquito dies on contact with a treated net, under the nets in place now | 0–0.56 | `calculate_dn0` on the current net mix ([Nets and dn0](../04-estimint/nets-and-dn0.qmd)) |
| `dn0_future` | The same probability, under the campaign net | 0–0.56 | `calculate_dn0` on the campaign net mix |
| `Q0` | Human blood index | 0–1, typically 0.7–0.95 | Vector species bionomics |
| `phi_bednets` | Share of bites taken while people are in bed | 0–1, typically 0.6–0.9 | Vector species bionomics |
| `seasonal` | Transmission profile. 0 perennial, 1 strongly seasonal | 0 or 1 | The setting |
| `routine` | Routine (continuous) net distribution running alongside the campaign | 0 or 1 | The campaign |
| `itn_use` | ITN coverage now | 0–1 | Survey or programme data |
| `irs_use` | IRS coverage now | 0–1 | Programme data |
| `itn_future` | ITN coverage from the campaign onwards | 0–1 | The campaign |
| `irs_future` | IRS coverage from the campaign onwards | 0–1 | The campaign |
| `lsm` | Larval source management coverage from the campaign onwards | 0–1 | The campaign |

`dn0_use` and `itn_use` describe the nets between them. One is the lethality of the product,
the other the fraction of people sleeping under it, and the emulator reads them as a pair
rather than as independent knobs. Omitting any of the twelve raises a `ValueError` that names
the keys left out.

```{python}
covars = {
    "eir": 31.96, "dn0_use": 0.311, "dn0_future": 0.485,
    "Q0": 0.85, "phi_bednets": 0.80, "seasonal": 0,
    "routine": 0.0, "itn_use": 0.70, "irs_use": 0.0,
    "itn_future": 0.70, "irs_future": 0.0, "lsm": 0.0,
}

incomplete = {k: v for k, v in covars.items() if k != "lsm"}

try:
    artifact.predict([incomplete])
except ValueError as err:
    print(f"{type(err).__name__}: {err}")
```

## `_use` and `_future`

Three quantities appear twice. The `_use` suffix is the world before the campaign and the
`_future` suffix is the campaign itself, in force from day 3285 onwards, so `dn0_use` becomes
`dn0_future` when the net product changes and takes its lethality with it. `lsm` and `routine`
have no `_use` counterpart. They exist only as campaign quantities.

## The pre-campaign window

Five covariates (`dn0_future`, `itn_future`, `irs_future`, `lsm` and `routine`) are held at
zero for every timestep before the intervention day, whatever value is passed, and take that
value only from day 3285 onwards.

```{python}
print(artifact.preprocessing_config["after_intervention"])
```

Two scenarios that agree in the present and differ in every campaign field therefore have
feature matrices that are indistinguishable until the campaign starts.

```{python}
import numpy as np

withdraw = dict(covars, dn0_future=0.0, itn_future=0.0, irs_future=0.0, lsm=0.0, routine=0.0)
package  = dict(covars, dn0_future=0.55, itn_future=0.90, irs_future=0.60, lsm=0.30, routine=1.0)

X = artifact.prepare_inputs([withdraw, package])
identical = np.isclose(X[0], X[1]).all(axis=1)
first_difference = int(np.argmin(identical))

print(f"input shape          : {X.shape}")
print(f"rows identical to    : step {first_difference - 1}")
print(f"first differing step : {first_difference}")
print(f"identical before it  : {bool(identical[:first_difference].all())}")
```

The emulator cannot represent a larviciding programme that has been running for years, or a
routine distribution channel that predates the campaign, because whatever is put in either
begins at day 3285. The pre-campaign period is described entirely by `eir`, `dn0_use`,
`itn_use`, `irs_use`, `Q0`, `phi_bednets` and `seasonal`, and an existing larviciding
programme is already inside the estimated EIR.

::: {.callout-important}
## Future coverage

Leaving `itn_future` and `dn0_future` at zero does not mean *keep the nets as they are*. It
means *the nets are withdrawn from day 3285 onwards*. The same holds for `irs_future`. It does
not inherit `irs_use`. To model an existing programme continuing, restate it, setting
`itn_future` to the coverage the campaign sustains and `dn0_future` to the lethality of the
net. Note that the same trap has the same shape at
[`run_scenarios`](../06-scenarios/run-scenarios.qmd), where `net_type_future`, `itn_future`
and `irs_future` all default to nothing, so a `Scenario` that omits them withdraws the
intervention. The failure is silent. What comes back is a plausible trajectory of the wrong
scenario.
:::

## The time grid

Nothing about the time axis is passed in. The emulator reconstructs it from four numbers in
the checkpoint's preprocessing config, which are worth reading out rather than hard-coding.

```{python}
cfg = artifact.preprocessing_config

n_steps          = cfg["n_steps"]
window_size      = cfg["window_size"]
model_start_day  = cfg["model_start_day"]
intervention_day = cfg["intervention_day"]

print(f"n_steps          = {n_steps}")
print(f"window_size      = {window_size} days")
print(f"model_start_day  = {model_start_day}")
print(f"intervention_day = {intervention_day}")
```

The simulation behind the training data runs for longer than this, and its first six years are
burn-in and are discarded. What survives is `n_steps` windows of `window_size` days, beginning
at `model_start_day`.

```{python}
abs_t = model_start_day + window_size * np.arange(n_steps)
years = (abs_t - intervention_day) / 365
idx_y9 = int(np.argmin(np.abs(abs_t - intervention_day)))

print(f"abs_t  : day {abs_t[0]} to day {abs_t[-1]}")
print(f"years  : {years[0]:+.2f} to {years[-1]:+.2f}")
print(f"idx_y9 : {idx_y9}  (day {abs_t[idx_y9]})")
```

`abs_t` is the absolute simulation day of each window and `years` recentres it on the campaign,
which is the axis worth plotting against, negative before, positive after, and zero the day the
nets go out. `idx_y9` is the index of the window nearest the campaign, the ninth year of the
simulation, which is where the name comes from and where estiMINT's `prev_y9` is measured. At
day 3282 it is the last window before the switch, three days short of it.

Read the baseline off `idx_y9` and check the emulator there against the prevalence fed to the
pipeline, rather than off the mean of the pre-campaign years. Day 2190 sits exactly 1095 days
before the campaign, one mass-distribution cycle, so the baseline window opens on the previous
net distribution and closes on the next. It is not a flat equilibrium. Its annual means are
nowhere near `prev_y9`, and the shape it does have is plotted in
[Plotting trajectories](plotting.qmd).

## See also

These twelve covariates become a trajectory in [Calling the emulator](the-emulator.qmd), which
loads a checkpoint and runs a batch of scenarios through it. Please see [Nets and
dn0](../04-estimint/nets-and-dn0.qmd) for where `dn0_use` and `dn0_future` come from.
